title: Knowledge Check 2: Lessons 6-10
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 6-10 of the ai-power-user series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Which single question decides whether an output should be structured or written as prose?
options: How long the finished output needs to run in total
Which chat tool happened to produce the answer
Whether the answer happens to contain any numbers at all
Who reads it: a person, or a piece of software
questions.explanation: If a person alone will read and act on the output, prose carries it better. Once software, a tracker, or an automation must read it, a labeled shape becomes the point.

questions.question: For an output a downstream tool will read, what makes a fixed label shape more useful than correct prose?
options: The tool finds each value by its label instead of guessing
The prose version is usually factually wrong about the details
The labeled version needs no review before it ships downstream
The labeled version is shorter and cheaper to generate
questions.explanation: Prose is often right but unstable, with the owner or the date landing in a different place each time. Labels make every run the same shape, so nothing downstream has to hunt or guess.

questions.question: Why pin a limited field, such as priority, to a fixed set of allowed values?
options: It lets the tool invent a value whenever one is missing
It removes the need to define that field inside the prompt at all
It keeps values consistent so a tool can sort and filter cleanly
It makes the output shorter for a human to read
questions.explanation: An open text field collects different spellings and formats that a tool cannot group. Allowed values keep every run inside the same set, which is what makes sorting and filtering work.

questions.question: In a reusable prompt, where does most of the value come from?
options: The fresh material you paste into the blanks each run
The length of the template, which signals the effort behind it
The fixed frame, written once and reused unchanged
The number of slots, which covers more possible variations
questions.explanation: The frame, the role, format, tone, and criteria, is what makes the output the same shape run after run. The filling changes by nature, so the consistent part is what earns the template its keep.

questions.question: Why must the fresh input be clearly separated from the standing instructions inside a template?
options: So the model treats it as data for this run, not as a rule
So the template file stays shorter and much easier to store
So the slot can be left empty on runs with no new facts
So the review step can be dropped for that particular run
questions.explanation: A marked boundary tells the model which text is an instruction and which is today's material. Blend the two and a value can be read as a rule, changing the shape of the output.

questions.question: A task recurs often, but its shape changes from run to run. What is the right call?
options: Build the template anyway and force the task to fit the frame
Skip it, because a frame that keeps changing will not hold
Add more slots so every variation has its own placeholder
Build a separate template for each variation the task might take
questions.explanation: A reusable prompt pays off only when a task recurs and its frame stays stable across runs. When the shape keeps shifting, the fixed part is never reused, so the setup is wasted.

questions.question: What is the full cost of owning a workflow?
options: The build cost plus the ongoing effort to keep it working
The license fee for the software that runs the workflow
The one-time build cost alone, paid once at the very start
The training needed to teach a colleague to run the workflow
questions.explanation: A workflow is usually priced by its build, but owning it also carries a recurring maintenance cost. Inputs, tools, and the task drift, so the workflow needs periodic review and repair.

questions.question: Why can an unmaintained workflow create more risk than a one-off?
options: Because it runs longer and uses more of the tool's capacity
Because it cannot be edited once it has been saved
Because you trust it while its accuracy silently drifts down
Because one-off prompts are always more accurate than workflows
questions.explanation: A one-off is openly temporary, so you re-examine the task each time. A workflow that looks permanent invites you to stop checking, and that is when drift goes unnoticed.

questions.question: A task recurs weekly and saves about twenty minutes each run. Building the setup takes one hour, once. By the break-even question, what should you conclude?
options: The setup is never repaid, because a one-time build is a permanent loss
The setup is repaid after roughly three runs, so it creates value
The setup is repaid only if the task also changes shape each run
The setup cannot be judged without knowing the tool's monthly fee
questions.explanation: Break-even compares the build effort against the saving per run. Twenty minutes saved weekly repays a one-hour build in about three runs, and every run after that is profit.

questions.question: What is the value of keeping a changelog for a prompt or tool you reuse?
options: It records each change and its reason, so failures trace to one edit
It proves to collaborators that the work was careful, dated, and reviewed
It shows that the prompt was tested thoroughly before anyone used it
It captures every keystroke and setting so no detail is ever lost
questions.explanation: A changelog turns a degraded output into a lookup: a dated entry names the edit and the reason behind it, so the cause can be found rather than guessed. Testing and review are separate habits that a log does not replace.

questions.question: A change to a working prompt makes its output worse. What does going back to the baseline require?
options: That the failing version is deleted before anything else is attempted
That the most recent edit is reverted by rewriting the prompt from memory
That a saved copy of the good version still exists to return to
That a new tool is chosen to replace the one that misbehaved
questions.explanation: Rollback is possible only if the known-good version was kept intact rather than overwritten, because returning to it needs a copy that still exists. Deleting the bad version or rewriting from memory does not restore the working state.

questions.question: You add a capability to a prompt without breaking anything it already did. In the major, minor, patch vocabulary, what kind of change is that?
options: A major change, because any edit to a working prompt counts as breaking
A minor change, because capability grew while existing behavior held
A patch change, because it only touches one part of the prompt
A baseline change, because the new version becomes the known-good state
questions.explanation: The three-part vocabulary classifies a change by its effect: major breaks existing use, minor adds capability without breaking it, and patch fixes something without changing behavior. Adding capability while current behavior holds is a minor change.

questions.question: What makes a run of a workflow a dry run?
options: It produces full output, then stops before anything is sent or changed
It runs on invented sample data so that the real records are never touched
It sends the output to one test recipient before the full list
It skips the output checks entirely so the workflow finishes faster
questions.explanation: A dry run uses the real input and produces the real result, then halts before any send, post, schedule, or record change. Substituting fake data or partially sending misses the point: the value is seeing the genuine output at zero consequence.

questions.question: A workflow handles normal input correctly but miscounts when a field arrives unusually long. What does that illustrate?
options: A happy-path run, because normal inputs behave as expected
An edge case, a failure at the boundary of the input range
A rollback, because an earlier version of the prompt was restored
A dry run, because output was produced without being sent anywhere
questions.explanation: An edge case is a problem that appears only at an extreme of the operating range rather than in normal use, so correct ordinary runs say nothing about it. Deliberately feeding the awkward input is what surfaces the failure.

questions.question: Output is well formed, plausible, and confident. Why check it before it goes out?
options: Because the tool bills less when a person reviews the result first
Because readers consistently prefer a shorter final document
Because a check makes the whole workflow run faster overall
Because fluent output can be wrong in ways that still look normal
questions.explanation: Bad output from a fluent system rarely looks broken; it looks smooth and reasonable while a number, citation, or section is simply wrong. Checking specific claims against something verifiable is what separates a plausible result from a correct one.
